bib.title: Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship, Chapter 17: Smells and Heuristics

question: Which code smells and heuristics, gathered while refactoring, should a programmer check for when reading and writing code?
contributions: A catalogue of 66 coded heuristics in six categories: Comments (C1-C5), Environment (E1-E2), Functions (F1-F4), General (G1-G36), Java (J1-J3), Names (N1-N7), Tests (T1-T9).

results.claim: The list was compiled by refactoring several programs and recording the reason for each change; it is the author's judgement, not measured data.
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: I compiled this list by walking through several different programs and refactoring them.

results.claim: Names account for most of software's readability.
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: Names in software are 90 percent of what make software readable.

results.claim: Functions should take at most three arguments; more is very questionable.
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: More than three is very questionable and should be avoided with prejudice.

results.claim: Duplication is one of the most important rules in the book.
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: This is one of the most important rules in this book, and you should take it very seriously.

results.claim: Flag/selector arguments declare that a function does more than one thing and should be eliminated.
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: Boolean arguments loudly declare that the function does more than one thing.

results.claim: Magic numbers: hide raw numbers behind named constants, but obvious ones (5280.0, 8 hours, 2*PI) may stay raw.
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: In general it is a bad idea to have raw numbers in your code.

results.claim: Comments should say what the code cannot say for itself.
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: Comments should say things that the code cannot say for itself.

results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: When you see commented-out code, delete it!

results.claim: At most one switch per type of selection (ONE SWITCH rule).
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: There may be no more than one switch statement for a given type of selection.

results.claim: Passing the tests is not enough: the author must know why the solution is correct.
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: It is not good enough that it passes all the tests.

results.claim: Currency should be held in integers (or a Money class), not floating point.
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: Using floating point numbers to represent currency is almost criminal.

results.claim: Name length should scale with scope.
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: So the longer the scope of the name, the longer and more precise the name should be.

results.claim: Slow tests get dropped from the suite.
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: A slow test is a test that won't get run.

results.claim: The list is a value system, not a rule set; it is not complete.
results.setup: Martin, Clean Code ch.17, practitioner heuristic from refactoring several programs
results.quote: Clean code is not written by following a set of rules.

limits: Practitioner judgement from the author's own refactoring sessions; no empirical test of any heuristic is reported.
The author concedes the list is not complete and that following a list does not make clean code (Conclusion).
Examples are Java 5-era (J1-J3, G18, G14); several rules are language-specific, and the wildcard-import advice J1 conflicts with modern Python style (wildcard imports are discouraged).
Printed cross-references point to Appendix C p.409 and other chapters, which are not in this PDF.
practices: C1: Keep change histories and metadata (authors, dates, SPR numbers) out of comments; they belong in source control or the issue tracker (p.286)
C2: Update or delete an obsolete comment as soon as you find it (p.286)
C3: Do not write comments that restate the code (i++; // increment i) or Javadoc that says less than the signature (p.286)
C4: If a comment is worth writing, write it well: brief, correct grammar, not obvious (p.287)
C5: Delete commented-out code; source control remembers it (p.287)
E1: A build should be one trivial operation (check out, then one command) (p.287)
E2: All unit tests should run with one command (p.287)
F1: Functions take few arguments: none best, then one, two, three; more than three is very questionable (p.288)
F2: Avoid output arguments; change the state of the object the function is called on (p.288)
F3: Eliminate boolean (flag) arguments: they declare the function does more than one thing (p.288)
F4: Delete methods that are never called (p.288)
G1: One language per source file; minimise the number and extent of embedded languages (p.288)
G2: Implement the behaviour a reader would reasonably expect (least surprise), e.g. day-name parsing accepts abbreviations and ignores case (p.288-289)
G3: Test every boundary and corner case; do not trust intuition (p.289)
G4: Do not override safeties: warnings, failing tests, serialVersionUID (p.289)
G5: Duplication: one of the most important rules; fold copies into methods, polymorphism for repeated switch/if chains, Template Method or Strategy for similar algorithms (p.289-290)
G6: Keep higher-level and lower-level concepts in separate containers; do not fake a misplaced abstraction (Stack.percentFull) (p.290-291)
G7: Base classes should not know their derivatives (p.291)
G8: Keep interfaces small and tight; hide data, utilities, constants, temporaries (p.291-292)
G9: Delete dead code (never executed) (p.292)
G10: Declare variables near use; define private functions just below first use (p.292)
G11: Be consistent: do similar things the same way and name them alike (p.292)
G12: Remove clutter: unused variables, uncalled functions, empty constructors, uninformative comments (p.293)
G13: Do not couple things that do not depend on each other (general enums inside specific classes) (p.293)
G14: Feature Envy: a method should use its own class's data, not another object's accessors; exception when it keeps format out of the data class (p.293-294)
G15: Selector arguments (a dangling false) combine many functions into one; prefer many functions (p.294-295)
G16: Run-on expressions, Hungarian notation and magic numbers obscure intent (p.295)
G17: Put code where a reader would expect it (least surprise); name functions to reveal where totals are computed (p.295-296)
G18: Prefer non-static methods; make static only if it will never need to be polymorphic (p.296)
G19: Use explanatory variables: break calculations into well-named intermediate values; hard to overdo (p.296-297)
G20: Function names should say what they do (date.add(5) is unclear) (p.297)
G21: Understand the algorithm: passing the tests is not enough, you must know the solution is correct (p.297-298)
G22: Make logical dependencies physical: ask the other module (getMaxPageSize()) instead of assuming (PAGE_SIZE = 55) (p.298-299)
G23: Prefer polymorphism to if/else or switch/case; ONE SWITCH rule: no more than one switch per type of selection (p.299)
G24: Follow team coding standards; it does not matter where braces go so long as all agree (p.299-300)

G25: Replace magic numbers with named constants, except self-evident ones (5280.0, hourlyRate * 8, radius * Math.PI * 2); applies to any non-self-describing token such as 7777 and 'John Doe' (p.300-301)
G26: Be precise: check for null, check for other records, use integers or a Money class for currency, lock for concurrent updates (p.301)
G27: Enforce design decisions with structure (abstract base classes) over convention (switch on enum) (p.301)
G28: Encapsulate conditionals: if (shouldBeDeleted(timer)) (p.301)
G29: Avoid negative conditionals (p.302)
G30: Functions should do one thing (p.302)
G31: Hide no temporal coupling: pass each result to the next call (bucket brigade) so the order is forced (p.302-303)
G32: Don't be arbitrary: have a reason for structure and let the structure communicate it (p.303-304)
G33: Encapsulate boundary conditions (nextLevel = level + 1) in one place (p.304)
G34: Functions descend only one level of abstraction; splitting often uncovers new levels (p.304-306)
G35: Keep configurable data at high levels and pass it down (p.306)
G36: Avoid transitive navigation (Law of Demeter): a.getB().getC() (p.306-307)
J1: Use wildcard imports instead of long import lists (Java-specific) (p.307)
J2: Do not inherit constants through an interface; use a static import (p.307-308)
J3: Use enums, not public static final ints (p.308-309)
N1: Choose descriptive names; names are 90 percent of what makes software readable; re-evaluate as meanings drift (p.309-310)
N2: Name at the level of abstraction of the class (connect(connectionLocator), not dial(phoneNumber)) (p.311)
N3: Use standard nomenclature: pattern names, toString, the project's ubiquitous language (p.311-312)
N4: Unambiguous names, even if long, when the function is called from one place (renamePageAndOptionallyAllReferences) (p.312)
N5: Name length should grow with scope: i is fine in a five-line scope (p.312)
N6: Avoid encodings (m_, f, vis_ prefixes, Hungarian) (p.312-313)
N7: Names should describe side effects (getOos creates the stream: createOrReturnOos) (p.313)
T1: A suite should test everything that could possibly break; 'that seems like enough' is not a metric (p.313)
T2: Use a coverage tool (p.313)
T3: Do not skip trivial tests (p.313)
T4: An ignored test records a question about an ambiguity in requirements (p.313)
T5: Test boundary conditions (p.314)
T6: Exhaustively test near bugs; bugs congregate (p.314)
T7: Patterns of failure are revealing (p.314)
T8: Test coverage patterns can be revealing (p.314)
T9: Tests should be fast; slow tests get dropped (p.314)

terms.definition: The methods of a class should be interested in the variables and functions of the class they belong to, and not the variables and functions of other classes.
There may be no more than one switch statement for a given type of selection.
An argument (boolean, enum, integer) used to select the behavior of the function.
Any token that has a value that is not self-describing.
Modules know only about their immediate collaborators and do not know the navigation map of the whole system.
Each function produces a result that the next function needs, so there is no reasonable way to call them out of order.
